Read About Vilnius

Vilnius is the baroque capital of the Baltics — a city of 65 churches crammed into one of Europe's largest surviving medieval old towns, built by a succession of rulers who left behind Gothic towers, Renaissance courtyards, and Baroque facades so exuberant they look almost improbable against the northern sky. For centuries it occupied an uneasy place at the crossroads of empires, absorbed by Russia, occupied by Napoleon, renamed by Poland, annihilated by the Nazis, and folded into the Soviet Union — yet it survives today as the independent capital of a country that sang its way to freedom.

The Founding Legend

The city owes its origin to a dream. In 1323, Grand Duke Gediminas camped on the confluence of the Neris and Vilnia rivers after a successful hunt. That night he dreamed of an iron wolf howling with the strength of a hundred wolves from a hilltop above the river. When he consulted the pagan high priest, he was told the wolf represented a great city that would be "famous the world over." Gediminas established his capital there and named it after the Vilnia River.

Whether or not the dream is myth, the choice of site was inspired. The hill gave the city's defenders a clear view over two river valleys; the rivers provided trade routes west to the Baltic and east into Russia. Within decades, Vilnius had grown into the capital of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania — at its medieval peak, the largest state in Europe, stretching from the Baltic Sea to within a hundred miles of the Black Sea.

The Grand Duchy

The Grand Duchy of Lithuania that radiated from Vilnius was an unusual empire for its time — a multi-ethnic, multilingual polity that governed Lithuanians, Belarusians, Ukrainians, Russians, Poles, and Jews with a degree of tolerance remarkable for medieval Europe. Its official language was not Lithuanian but Ruthenian, an ancestor of modern Belarusian and Ukrainian. Its coat of arms — the armored knight on horseback, still used by Lithuania today — was designed to appeal to the Slavic populations it absorbed as much as to its Baltic rulers.

Under Grand Duke Vytautas the Great in the early 15th century, the duchy reached its maximum extent, its western border touching Poland at the Baltic. This was also Vilnius's first golden age: the Palace of the Grand Dukes was expanded, the Cathedral was rebuilt, and the city drew craftsmen, merchants, and scholars from across Europe. The Jagiellonian dynasty, which ruled both Lithuania and Poland through a personal union from 1386, made Vilnius one of the most cosmopolitan cities of central Europe.

Jerusalem of Lithuania

No story of Vilnius can pass over its Jewish history. From the 15th century onward, Vilnius became one of the great centers of Jewish learning in the world — a city where the quality of rabbinical scholarship was so extraordinary that it earned the name "Jerusalem of Lithuania." At its peak before the Second World War, nearly a quarter of Vilnius's population was Jewish, and the city was home to over a hundred synagogues, dozens of Jewish publishers and newspapers, and the YIVO Institute for Jewish Research, which sought to document and preserve Yiddish culture.

The city's most celebrated scholar was Elijah ben Solomon Zalman, known as the Vilna Gaon (the Genius of Vilna), born in 1720. The Gaon was a prodigious intellect who could recite the entire Torah by the age of three and went on to write over seventy major works covering every branch of Jewish learning. He declined an offer to become rabbi of any community, preferring a life of uninterrupted study. His reputation was so great that his descendants are still celebrated across the Jewish world, and scholars make pilgrimages to his tomb to this day.

The Holocaust destroyed this world almost completely. The German army occupied Vilnius in June 1941; by the end of that year, most of the city's Jewish population had been transported to Paneriai, a forest clearing seven kilometers south of the city, and shot. By 1943 the Vilna Ghetto, which had held over 20,000 people, was liquidated. Of the roughly 100,000 Jews killed at Paneriai, approximately 70,000 were Lithuanian Jews. The city that had been Jerusalem of Lithuania for four centuries was silent.

Contested City

If Vilnius's Jewish history is the city's saddest chapter, its Polish-Lithuanian chapter is perhaps its most contested. For much of the 19th and early 20th century, the city's dominant language was Polish — the language of the educated class, the Catholic Church, and the local nobility. The great Polish Romantic poet Adam Mickiewicz, whose statue stands near the city center, was born in a village near Vilnius and called the city his home. He began his masterwork "Pan Tadeusz" with the words "Lithuania, my homeland" — and he meant a Lithuania that spoke Polish.

When both Poland and Lithuania declared independence after World War One, both claimed Vilnius. The city was seized by the Polish general Lucjan Żeligowski in a staged "mutiny" in 1920 and incorporated into Poland, remaining the Polish city of Wilno until 1939. It was only after the Soviet Union occupied eastern Poland in September 1939, as part of the Nazi-Soviet Pact's division of Europe, that the city was handed to Lithuania — briefly, before the Soviets occupied Lithuania in its entirety in 1940.

The tensions between Polish and Lithuanian claims on the city remained sensitive for decades after independence. Today the two countries have largely reconciled over the shared experience of Soviet occupation, and the city's Polish minority — still several percent of the population — is a recognized community with its own schools and cultural institutions.

Soviet Vilnius

Under Soviet rule, Vilnius was transformed from a multicultural borderland city into the capital of the Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic. The Jewish community had been annihilated; the Polish upper class had largely emigrated; ethnic Lithuanians, many relocated from villages and provincial towns, became the city's new population. Entire new districts of concrete apartment blocks rose on the city's outskirts. The Cathedral was converted into a picture gallery; the historic churches were closed, repurposed, or turned into warehouses and concert halls.

Yet Vilnius under Soviet rule also experienced a quiet cultural resistance. Lithuanian language and folk culture were preserved through choral societies, folk ensembles, and the amber and linen craft traditions that the Soviets found safely folkloric. The dissident movement, while suppressed, never fully disappeared. And Vilnius harbored the kind of underground Catholic devotion — at the Gate of Dawn, where pilgrims continued to pray at the icon of the Virgin Mary despite official atheism — that the Soviets could never quite extinguish.

The Singing Revolution

The independence movement that ended Soviet rule in Lithuania is called the Singing Revolution because it began with song. In 1987 the first mass protest in decades took place in Vilnius. In 1988 the Lithuanian movement Sąjūdis was founded and quickly attracted hundreds of thousands of supporters. In January 1989 the Lithuanian flag — yellow, green, and red — flew over Gediminas Tower for the first time in nearly fifty years.

The most dramatic moment came on August 23, 1989, the 50th anniversary of the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact. An estimated two million people joined hands in a human chain — the Baltic Way — stretching 675 kilometers from Vilnius through Riga in Latvia to Tallinn in Estonia, a silent demonstration of peaceful defiance that captured the world's attention.

Lithuania declared independence on March 11, 1990, becoming the first Soviet republic to do so. The Soviet response was brutal: in January 1991, Soviet troops stormed the Vilnius TV Tower and the Parliament building. Fourteen unarmed civilians were killed defending the Parliament, their bodies becoming symbols of the price of freedom. The Soviet coup against Gorbachev failed in August 1991, and Lithuania's independence was internationally recognized. The country joined the European Union and NATO in 2004.

Baroque Capital

Despite everything — plagues, fires, wars, occupations — Vilnius's Old Town has survived with its medieval street pattern largely intact, and it is this survival that earned it UNESCO World Heritage status in 1994. The city's defining visual character is Baroque, the style that swept through Catholic Europe in the 17th and 18th centuries with its characteristic drama, exuberance, and emotional intensity.

The greatest Baroque interior in the Baltics is St. Peter and Paul Church, whose nave and chapels are covered with over 2,000 white stucco figures — a collaboration between Italian sculptors and local craftsmen that took over twenty years to complete. The patron, Grand Hetman Michał Kazimierz Pac, reportedly spent so much of his fortune on the church that he died in debt, but left behind something that still stops visitors in their tracks three and a half centuries later.

The red-brick facade of St. Anne's Church, built in the late 15th century from 33 different types of custom-shaped brick, represents the Gothic virtuosity that preceded the Baroque flowering. When Napoleon saw it in 1812 during his advance on Moscow, he reportedly said he wished he could carry it to Paris in the palm of his hand. He didn't, but his soldiers camped in the Bernardine Church next door, and his horses were stabled in the Cathedral.

Užupis Republic

In 1997, a neighborhood of artists, squatters, and bohemians on the east bank of the Vilnia River declared itself the Independent Republic of Užupis. The republic has its own president (artist Romas Lileikis), its own national anthem, its own army of eleven soldiers, and its own constitution — a document of forty-one articles that includes the rights of cats to be cats, dogs to be dogs, and people to be idle, to love, to make mistakes, and to know nothing.

The constitution is translated into over fifty languages and inscribed on bronze plaques along Paupio gatve. On April 1st each year, Independence Day, the republic's symbolic border crossing at Užupio gatve is manned by border guards who stamp passports and bestow citizenship on visitors. The president gives a speech. The army stands at attention.

None of it is legally recognized, of course. But Užupis is also genuinely one of the most interesting neighborhoods in the Baltics — a compact maze of studios, galleries, street art, and riverside cafes that has managed to retain its artist character despite rapidly rising rents. The Angel of Užupis, a golden figure atop a tall column, watches over it all with the serenity of a place that has decided not to take itself too seriously.

Vilnius Today

Modern Vilnius is a city of about 600,000 — small enough to walk across its historic center in an afternoon, large enough to have a genuine restaurant and nightlife scene. Since EU accession in 2004, the city has attracted investment, rebuilt its economy, and become increasingly prosperous, though income inequality and the legacy of Soviet-era concrete suburbs remain challenges.

The city has invested heavily in its historic center: the Palace of the Grand Dukes, demolished in the early 19th century, was painstakingly reconstructed on its original foundations between 1988 and 2018. The KGB Museum occupies the actual former KGB building, preserved exactly as it operated — a stark reminder that independence is recent enough that the prison cells and interrogation rooms still exist. And the Vilna Gaon Jewish State Museum works to document and honor a community that was almost entirely destroyed within living memory.

What makes Vilnius unusual among Eastern European capitals is the sense that its history is not yet settled, its wounds not yet healed, and its character not yet fixed — that it remains, in some essential way, still becoming what it will eventually be. That quality of becoming, of a city still working out what it is, gives Vilnius an energy that more self-assured capitals sometimes lack.
